title: Solar Charge Controller Size Calculator | Wattlyst
meta: Find the amp rating of your PWM or MPPT solar charge controller from panel watts and battery voltage, with a safety margin and cold-weather Voc.
author: ali-ahmad

sections.h2: What size charge controller do I need?
p: For an MPPT controller, divide the total panel watts by the battery bank voltage and add the safety margin. 1,000 W on a 24 V bank is 52.1 A after the 1.25 margin, so the controller to buy is the next size sold, 60 A. The amps are the current going into the battery, which is why the bank voltage matters so much: the same array on twice the voltage needs half the amps.

The second check is voltage. Panels in series add their open-circuit voltage, and on a cold clear morning it rises above the label value. The controller's maximum PV input voltage on its datasheet must stay above the string's open-circuit voltage on the coldest morning in your area; this calculator sizes the amps only, so count the panels in series against the datasheet before you buy.

sections.h2: MPPT charge controller size for 12 V, 24 V and 48 V
p: The examples below show how fast the amps climb on a low bank voltage: 600 W on 12 V already needs 62.5 A and an 80 A controller, while 2,000 W on 48 V needs only 52.1 A and a 60 A controller. Large MPPT controllers are expensive, so a bigger array is usually paired with a higher bank voltage rather than a bigger controller. The table shows the controller for arrays from 500 W to 3,500 W on a 48 V bank.
A hybrid solar inverter has its MPPT built in; check its maximum PV watts and voltage the same way. This page is for a separate controller on a battery system.

sections.h2: How many watts can a 60 A MPPT handle?
p: Work the formula backwards: controller amps × bank volts ÷ the margin. A 60 A MPPT on 24 V covers the 1,000 W array above with 52.1 A needed, and on 48 V it covers about 2,000 W (52.1 A). On half the voltage it is limited to roughly half the watts. Most makers also print a maximum PV watts per bank voltage on the datasheet; the lower of the two numbers is the limit.

sections.h2: PWM vs MPPT: which charge controller and how is each sized?
p: A PWM controller connects the panel almost directly to the battery, so the panel runs at the battery voltage and the controller only has to carry the panel current. It is sized from the short-circuit current: 2 panels of 10 A Isc in parallel need 25 A with the margin, so a 30 A PWM. It only suits panels whose working voltage matches the battery, which rules out today's large high-voltage panels on a 12 V or 24 V bank.

An MPPT controller converts a higher panel voltage down to the battery voltage and turns the spare volts into extra amps, so it harvests more from the same panels, especially in winter and in the morning. It costs more per amp, but for any array over a few hundred watts, or any modern panel on a small bank, MPPT is the right choice.

sections.h2: Charge controller for 1,000 W of solar
p: On a 24 V bank 1,000 W needs 52.1 A, so a 60 A MPPT controller; on twice the voltage the same array needs half that. 1,500 W on 24 V needs 78.2 A and an 80 A controller. If you plan to add panels later, buy the controller for the final array, because the amps rise with every panel.

faq.q: What size charge controller do I need for 1,000 W of solar?
faq.a: On a 24 V bank, 52.1 A with the margin, so a 60 A MPPT controller. On twice the voltage the same panels need about half the amps; on half the voltage about twice.

faq.q: How many watts can a 60 A MPPT charge controller handle?
faq.a: About 1,000 W on a 24 V bank (52.1 A needed) and about 2,000 W on 48 V (52.1 A). Check the maker's maximum PV watts per bank voltage as well; the lower figure is the limit.

faq.q: How do I size a PWM charge controller?
faq.a: Multiply the short-circuit current of one panel by the number of panels in parallel and by the 1.25 margin. 2 panels of 10 A Isc need 25 A, so a 30 A PWM.

faq.q: PWM or MPPT: which should I buy?
faq.a: MPPT for any modern panel on a 12 V or 24 V bank, for arrays over a few hundred watts, and wherever winter output matters; PWM only for small panels whose voltage matches the battery. MPPT harvests more from the same panels.

faq.q: Does the charge controller size depend on the battery voltage?
faq.a: Yes, for MPPT: amps = watts ÷ bank volts. 2,000 W needs 52.1 A on 48 V but would need twice that on half the voltage, so a higher bank voltage means a smaller, cheaper controller.

faq.q: Does this calculator check the panel voltage (Voc)?
faq.a: No. It sizes the amps only. Add the open-circuit voltage of the panels in series, allow for the rise on a cold morning, and make sure the controller's maximum PV input voltage on its datasheet is above that figure.

faq.q: What if the result is above the largest controller size?
faq.a: Split the array over two controllers, or move to a higher bank voltage, which halves the amps. Standard sizes end at 100 A in this calculator.

key_facts: MPPT charge controller amps = total panel watts ÷ battery voltage × a 1.25 margin: 1,000 W on 24 V needs 52.1 A, so a 60 A controller; the same watts on half the voltage would need twice the amps.
A 60 A MPPT handles about 2,000 W of panels on a 48 V bank (52.1 A needed) but only about 1,000 W on 24 V (52.1 A), because the amps are set by watts ÷ volts.
PWM charge controller amps = panel short-circuit current × panels in parallel × 1.25: 2 panels of 10 A Isc need 25 A, so a 30 A PWM controller.
Standard controller sizes are limited; above the largest size the array must be split over two controllers or moved to a higher bank voltage.
mistakes: Sizing an MPPT from the panel amps. An MPPT delivers more amps to the battery than the panels make, so size it from watts ÷ bank volts, as the calculator does.
Ignoring the open-circuit voltage. Panels in series on a cold morning can exceed the controller's maximum PV voltage and destroy it; check the string voltage against the datasheet.
Putting a large modern panel on a PWM controller with a 12 V battery. The panel's working voltage is far above the battery, and a PWM throws the difference away.
Leaving no margin. Clear cold days push panels above their label; the 1.25 margin keeps the controller under its limit.
Buying for today's panels only. Adding panels later raises the amps; size the controller for the array you will end up with.

fields.name: type
fields.label: Controller type
fields.hint: MPPT is sized from the array watts and the battery voltage. PWM is sized from the panel short-circuit current, because it passes the panel current straight to the battery.

fields.name: panel_w
fields.label: Total panel watts
fields.hint: Add up the label watts of every panel on this controller. Used for MPPT.

fields.name: battery_v
fields.label: Battery bank voltage
fields.hint: The bank the controller charges. A higher bank voltage halves the controller amps for the same watts.

fields.name: isc
fields.label: Short-circuit current of one panel (Isc)
fields.hint: From the panel label, marked Isc. Used for PWM only.

fields.name: n_parallel
fields.label: Panels or strings in parallel
fields.hint: How many panels (or series strings) are wired in parallel into the controller. Used for PWM only.

fields.name: margin
fields.label: Safety margin
fields.hint: Panels can briefly give more than their label on cold, clear days; the margin keeps the controller below its limit. A decimal like one point two five.

examples.text: 1,000 W ÷ 24 V × 1.25 = 52.1 A. Next size sold: 60 A MPPT.

examples.title: 1,500 W on a 24 V bank, MPPT
examples.text: 1,500 W ÷ 24 V × 1.25 = 78.2 A, so an 80 A MPPT. Moving the bank to twice the voltage would halve the amps.

examples.title: 2,000 W on a 48 V bank, MPPT
examples.text: 2,000 W ÷ 48 V × 1.25 = 52.1 A, so a 60 A MPPT. The same array on half the voltage would need twice the amps and a bigger controller.

examples.title: 2 panels of 10 A Isc in parallel, PWM
examples.text: 10 A × 2 in parallel × 1.25 = 25 A, so a 30 A PWM controller. The panel voltage must match the battery bank for PWM to work well.

examples.title: 600 W on a 12 V bank, MPPT
examples.text: 600 W ÷ 12 V × 1.25 = 62.5 A, so an 80 A MPPT. A small bank voltage makes even a modest array expensive to control; twice the voltage would need half the amps.

content.answer: 1,000 W of solar panels on a 24 V battery needs an MPPT solar charge controller of at least 52.1 A, so buy the next size sold, a 60 A controller. MPPT amps = total panel watts ÷ battery volts × a safety margin of 1.25; a PWM controller is sized from the panel short-circuit current × panels in parallel × the same margin.

formula.text: MPPT: A = P_array ÷ V_battery × m; PWM: A = Isc × N_parallel × m; buy the next standard size ≥ A
lines: P_array = total label watts of the panels on the controller
Isc = short-circuit current of one panel from its label
N_parallel = panels or strings wired in parallel
m = safety margin for cold, clear days

content.safety: The controller, DC fuses or breakers, cables and battery connections carry high DC current; have a licensed electrician or a certified solar installer wire them, connect the battery before the panels, and never exceed the controller's maximum PV voltage.
